I started with ABV, moved to trim. I finally decided I was sick of getting burnt hands and feeling like I was losing THC in the left overs...so i started cooking with extracts.

All of a sudden my edibles were always the right potency, never had any sticks or grit in them, and the taste of the cannabis disappeared HEAPS.

So how do you cook?
Hey, I like cooking with QWISO hash. What do you cook with?

I have a multi step process that makes a really potent cannabutter, then I cook with that. I use alcohol but not isopropyl, Everclear is my choice because any residual amounts aren't toxic. It takes me at least twenty four hours from start to brownies but it's worth it. My potency still varies a bit depending on the flowers I use but I don't have sticks or grit. I strain my butter through cheesecloth before cooking with it.
So you make QWISO with everclear and then cook with the extract? Do you use the same amount of extract each time?

Not quite, here's the short version:

I decarboxylate my bud and sugar leaves, twenty minutes in a 200 oven. Next the slightly crispy cannabis goes into a blender with the grain alcohol, I add just enough to let it grind then I blend it for a good thirty seconds. Next the slurry goes into quart canning jars along with sticks of butter, the tops are loosely applied. four of these at a time fit into a water bath in my crockpot on low, I'll stir them every fifteen minutes or so at first, every hour or two after that. If the alcohol cooks off early I'll add more butter. The next day I cook them for the last hour with the tops off to remove any remaining grain alcohol. I drain the butter through the cheesecloth (or jelly bag, used for making preserves, much easier) to get the grit out and I'm done. I use the butter in a commercial brownie mix instead of oil and I underbake them just a bit because they survive the freezer better that way.

tl,dr; I use alcohol in my extraction process but I don't bother to separate it into a tincture first. QWISO requires the faster extraction properties of isopropyl alcohol, you need longer exposure to methyl alcohol to get the same results.
That's an interesting way to go about it. Do you find you get much taste from the chlorophyll?

No, the decarboxylation stage removes a lot of that flavor, the long simmer time cooks out the rest. I like the remaining cannabis flavor, it has an appealing toasted quality. If I need to use a lot of low potency cannabis (I'm in Oregon, this no longer happens) then I use a jelly bag and steep my weed, like tea, before the decarboxylation step. THC is not a water soluble molecule, even steam won't touch it, so you won't lose potency by removing your unpleasant flavors first.
